asset.title: RAG Ingestion and Retrieval: From Passages to Evidence Selection
asset.evidence_note: The reference chunks cover RAG ingestion, passage vectorization, query-based retrieval, and evidence selection for a learning objective. They support an easy lesson without generating questions.
learning_objectives: Describe how passages become vectors during RAG ingestion.
Explain how a learning objective selects evidence through vector similarity.
Recognize that retrieval scores are not proof of correctness and that citations require human review.

sections.heading: RAG Ingestion: Passage to Vector
sections.text: RAG ingestion starts by extracting text from an allowed document. The application divides the text into passages and stores each passage with an identifier, document name, and page reference. An embedding service maps passage text to a numeric vector. The passage vector and its source metadata belong together because a vector without its text cannot supply inspectable evidence. A small overlap between neighboring passages can preserve context at a boundary, but overlap also creates repeated text.

sections.heading: Retrieval: How a Learning Objective Selects Evidence
sections.text: At request time, the application embeds the learning objective using a compatible embedding configuration. It compares the query vector with stored passage vectors and ranks candidates by similarity. The selected passages accompany the objective in a text-generation request. The generator should use those passages to explain a covered concept or write an answerable exercise. Retrieval supplies external evidence; it does not update the language model's parameters and does not itself prove the final explanation correct.

sections.heading: Interpreting Ranked Passages and Scores
sections.text: In a RAG ingestion example with eight passages and a retrieval limit of three, a request about citations should rank citation passages ahead of unrelated interface notes. The evidence record should preserve the actual ranked passages and similarity scores. A score measures the comparison used by this retrieval configuration; it is not a calibrated probability that the answer is correct. If every passage is returned, the run demonstrates context supply but does not demonstrate selective ranking. A human still checks whether the selected passages cover the requested objective.

sections.heading: Evidence Boundaries and Compatibility
sections.text: An evidence boundary is crossed when a requested conclusion cannot be derived from the supplied material. If a learner asks for a clinical treatment dosage while the course notes only explain retrieval systems, the notes provide no clinical evidence; the appropriate response is to report insufficient evidence. Embedding compatibility also matters: vectors must have the same dimension before coordinates can be compared, but matching dimensions alone are insufficient because different models can use different semantic spaces. A useful failure message explains why reindexing is needed instead of silently comparing incompatible vectors.

sections.heading: Reviewed Text Versions Are Separate from Retrieval
sections.text: Embedding compatibility and a reviewed text version are different concerns. Reindexing changes the vectors used by future retrieval, but it does not retrospectively repair or approve an already generated explanation. The earlier explanation remains associated with its original source passages and generation settings. If a reviewer later edits that explanation, the system creates a new text version. Keeping these histories separate lets an observer distinguish a retrieval configuration change from a correction to teaching content.

asset.visual_prompt: A simple diagram showing a document split into passages, each passage linked to a numeric vector and source metadata. An arrow from a learning objective passes through an embedding step to a query vector, which is compared with stored passage vectors to rank and select a few passages for a text-generation request. Include a small separate box labeled 'human review' and a note that similarity scores are not proof of correctness.

# CA1 demonstration course: evidence, retrieval, and reviewed learning materials

This is self-authored synthetic teaching material for a software demonstration. It is not an official course handout, a research result, or a benchmark of any model. Its examples deliberately separate evidence from claims about quality. The notes contain several topics so that the application must select a subset of passages for a request. A successful demonstration does not establish accuracy for real students.

## RAG ingestion and retrieval

RAG ingestion begins with extracting text from an allowed document. The application divides the text into passages and stores each passage with an identifier, document name, and page reference. An embedding service maps passage text to a numeric vector. The passage vector and its source metadata belong together: a vector without its text cannot supply a reader with inspectable evidence. A small overlap between neighboring passages can preserve context at a boundary, although overlap also creates repeated text.

An evidence boundary is crossed when a requested conclusion cannot be derived from the supplied material. Suppose a learner asks for a clinical treatment dosage while the course notes only explain retrieval systems. The notes provide no clinical evidence. The appropriate response is to report insufficient evidence and avoid inventing a dosage or an exercise that presents one as correct. The generator may explain that the relevant source material is missing. A provider outage or malformed response is an operational failure, not a successful refusal based on evidence.

## Embedding compatibility and index versions

Embedding compatibility concerns the relationship between stored document vectors and a new query vector. Vectors must have the same dimension before their coordinates can be compared. Matching dimensions alone are insufficient: two models can use different semantic spaces while producing the same number of coordinates. A query from one space must not be assumed compatible with passages embedded by another model.
